cards.a: Set the dividers to 38'.4 on the latitude scale at the side, step in from the nearest printed parallel and pencil a short line; set them to 33'.6 on the longitude scale at the top or bottom and step in from the nearest meridian, using a straight edge or plotter. The position is the crossing. Check the hemisphere, and that the minutes increase in the direction you expect.

cards.q: Your leg will take 40 minutes. What do you put in the course-to-steer triangle?
cards.a: Vectors for the same period: 40 minutes of tide, so rate × 40/60, and 40 minutes of boat speed. Any period works so long as both use it. Over more than an hour, or where the stream changes, work hour by hour or use the resultant of each hour's tide.

cards.q: What causes tides?
cards.a: The gravitational pull of the moon and, to a lesser extent, the sun on the oceans, plus the centrifugal effect of the earth-moon system. The moon dominates, so the tidal day is about 24 h 50 min and there are usually two high waters a day, roughly 12 h 25 min apart.

cards.q: What are spring and neap tides, and when do they occur?
cards.a:
Springs — the sun and moon pull in line at new and full moon, giving the largest range: highest highs and lowest lows.
Neaps — at the first and last quarter the pulls are at right angles, giving the smallest range. There is a lag of about two days after the phase of the moon.

cards.q: Define chart datum and say what UK charts use.
cards.a: The level from which charted depths and drying heights are measured. On UK Admiralty charts it is approximately Lowest Astronomical Tide (LAT), the lowest level predictable under average meteorological conditions, so the sea very rarely falls below the charted depth.

cards.q: What are MHWS, MHWN, MLWN and MLWS?
cards.a: Mean High Water Springs, Mean High Water Neaps, Mean Low Water Neaps and Mean Low Water Springs — the average heights above chart datum of high and low waters at springs and neaps.

cards.q: What is the height of tide, and what is the range?
cards.a: The height of tide is the height of the sea surface above chart datum at a given moment. The range is the difference between the heights of successive high and low waters.

cards.q: What is the depth of water at a place?
cards.a: Charted depth + height of tide.

cards.q: How much water is there over a patch that dries 1.8 m when the height of tide is 4.2 m?
cards.a: Height of tide − drying height = 4.2 − 1.8 = 2.4 m.

cards.q: How do you work out clearance under the keel?
cards.a: Charted depth + height of tide − draught. Then subtract a safety margin for swell, squat, chart accuracy and barometric effect before you decide to go.

cards.q: What datum are charted heights and vertical clearances measured from?
cards.a: Heights of lights, beacons and land features are above MHWS. Vertical clearances under bridges and overhead cables are above HAT on new-edition Admiralty charts and MHWS on older ones — the title block says which. Real clearance = charted clearance + the height datum − height of tide, which is normally more than the charted figure.

cards.q: State the rule of twelfths.
cards.a: Between low and high water the tide rises by 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 then 1 twelfths of the range in each successive sixth of the tidal duration.

cards.q: LW 1.2 m at 0600, HW 5.4 m at 1215. Estimate the height at 0900.
cards.a: Range 5.4 − 1.2 = 4.2 m, so a twelfth is 0.35 m. Duration 6 h 15 min, so each sixth is 62½ min. 0900 is 180 min after LW, which is 2.9 sixths — call it 3. Risen 1+2+3 = 6 twelfths = 2.1 m, so the height is 1.2 + 2.1 = about 3.3 m above chart datum.

cards.q: What are the limitations of the rule of twelfths?
cards.a: It assumes a symmetrical, roughly sinusoidal curve and a six-hour rise. It is unreliable where the curve is distorted — the Solent and Poole with their double high waters, the Thames, and many rivers and estuaries. For anything tight use the tidal curve.

cards.q: Describe how you use a standard port tidal curve to find the height at a given time.
cards.a:
Take HW and LW times and heights from the tables.
Fill in the hour boxes with HW time in the centre.
Draw the sloping line joining the LW height on the lower scale to the HW height on the upper scale.
Enter the graph at the time wanted, go up to the curve (spring, neap, or interpolated by range), across to the sloping line, then up or down to the height scale — the top and bottom scales are the same graduation.
Check the diagram's reference: a few ports, including Portland, Poole and Christchurch, have curves drawn about LW, so the centre box is LW time.

cards.q: How do you use the tidal curve the other way — to find the time at which a given height occurs?
cards.a: Enter at the height on the sloping line, go up (or down) to the curve, then across to the time scale. Do it for both the rise and the fall to get the window during which you have enough water.

cards.q: Which curve do you use when the range is between springs and neaps?
cards.a: Interpolate between the spring and neap curves in proportion to the day's actual range compared with the mean spring and mean neap ranges printed on the diagram.

cards.q: What is a standard port and what is a secondary port?
cards.a: A standard port has its own full tide tables and tidal curve. A secondary port is worked out from a nominated standard port by applying tabulated time differences and height differences from the almanac.

cards.q: How do you work out HW time and height at a secondary port?
cards.a:
Take the standard port's HW time and height.
The table gives time differences at two tabulated HW times: interpolate between them on the standard port's actual HW time.
It gives height differences at the standard port's MHWS and MHWN (and MLWN and MLWS): interpolate on the standard port's actual height.
Apply both differences.
Then work the height on the standard port's curve, with the secondary port's HW time in the centre box and its own HW and LW heights on the scales, unless the almanac prints a curve for the secondary port itself.

cards.q: What does 'the tide is making' or 'the tide is taking off' mean?
cards.a:
Making — the ranges are increasing day by day towards springs.
Taking off — the ranges are decreasing towards neaps.

cards.q: What is the difference between a tidal gate and a tidal window?
cards.a: A tidal gate is a place you can only pass at certain states of tide — a race, an overfall, a bridge, a sill, a bar. A tidal window is the span of time during which you have enough depth or a fair stream to do so. Plan the passage around the gates.

cards.q: What is a sill, and what must you check before entering a marina with one?
cards.a:
A wall across the entrance that retains water inside at low tide. Check the height of the sill above chart datum,
your draught,
and the height of tide at your arrival and departure times,
and remember you may be locked in as well as out.

cards.q: What effects can make the actual tide differ from the prediction?
cards.a: Barometric pressure — roughly 0.01 m per millibar of departure from 1013 mb, so 30 mb below it raises the level about 0.3 m and a high depresses it; strong or prolonged wind can pile water up on a coast (a surge) or hold it back; heavy river flow raises levels in an estuary. Never plan on the last 0.2 m.

cards.q: Why is the ebb usually more dangerous than the flood for a small yacht?
cards.a: The ebb runs out against the prevailing swell over shoals and bars, steepening and breaking the seas, and it takes you offshore away from shelter if you break down. Many harbour bars are only safe on the flood.

cards.q: Where do you find the time zone of a set of tide tables, and why does it matter?
cards.a: In the heading of the table — UK Admiralty tables are in UT (GMT). In British Summer Time you must add one hour to every tabulated time. Getting this wrong is the single most common tidal error.

cards.q: Which tidal curve do you use for a secondary port?
cards.a: The standard port's curve, unless the almanac prints one for the secondary port itself. Work out the secondary port's HW and LW times and heights first, then put its HW time in the centre box and its own HW and LW heights on the height scales. Choose the spring or neap curve, or interpolate, on the standard port's range.

cards.q: You draw 1.8 m and want 1.0 m under the keel to cross a bar charted at 0.6 m. What height of tide do you need, and how do you find the window?
cards.a: Required height of tide = draught + clearance − charted depth = 1.8 + 1.0 − 0.6 = 2.2 m. Enter the tidal curve at 2.2 m on the sloping line, read across to the curve and down to the time scale on both the rise and the fall: the span between those two times is your tidal window.

cards.q: What are LAT and HAT, and where does each appear?
cards.a: Lowest and Highest Astronomical Tide — the extreme levels predictable under average meteorological conditions and any combination of astronomical conditions. Chart datum is at approximately LAT, so charted depths are almost never overstated. Vertical clearances under bridges and cables on new-edition Admiralty charts are above HAT. Neither is a limit the weather cannot beat.

cards.q: What is the difference between a tidal stream and a current?
cards.a: A tidal stream is the horizontal flow of water caused by the tide; it reverses predictably. A current is a non-tidal flow driven by wind, river outflow or ocean circulation, and it does not reverse.

cards.q: Define set and drift, and rate.
cards.a: Set is the direction the stream flows towards, in degrees true. Rate is its speed in knots. Drift is the distance the stream carries you over a stated period.

cards.q: How do you read a tidal diamond table?
cards.a: Find the diamond letter on the chart, then in the almanac read the row for the hour relative to HW at the named reference port. It gives the set in degrees true, and the rate for springs and for neaps. Interpolate for the actual range.

cards.q: A tidal stream atlas arrow reads 19,34. What does that mean?
cards.a: The rate is 1.9 knots at neaps and 3.4 knots at springs in the direction of the arrow, for that hour relative to HW at the atlas's reference port.

cards.q: How do you get the actual rate when the day is neither springs nor neaps?
cards.a: Interpolate between the neap and spring figures in proportion to the day's range compared with the mean neap and mean spring ranges. Many almanacs print a computation-of-rates diagram to do this graphically.

cards.q: Where do tidal streams run fastest?
cards.a:
Where the flow is squeezed: round headlands,
through narrows and channels,
over shallow banks,
and between islands. Streams are weaker in bays and close inshore, which is why you cheat the tide in the shallows.

cards.q: What is a tidal race and an overfall?
cards.a: Disturbed, steep and breaking water where a strong stream runs over an uneven bottom or round a headland, or where two streams meet. It can be dangerous out of proportion to the wind strength. Avoid it, or time your passage for slack water and a fair wind.

cards.q: What happens when wind and tide oppose one another?
cards.a: The waves become steeper, shorter and more likely to break — 'wind against tide'. The same wind with the tide gives a longer, easier sea. A gale against a spring ebb over a shoal is genuinely dangerous.

cards.q: What is a lee-bow tide and why do skippers like it?
cards.a: A tidal stream setting onto the leeward bow. The tide's vector is the same whichever tack you are on, so it is not free windward gain — the point is that on the lee-bow tack the stream carries you towards your windward objective rather than away from it, and the boat sails a heading closer to the track you need. When beating, work the tack that puts the tide on the lee bow.

cards.q: What is slack water, and does it coincide with high water?
cards.a: The short period when the stream is not running. It does not necessarily coincide with HW or LW: in some places the stream turns close to local high and low water, in others nearer mid-tide, and the difference can be two to three hours. Always take the timing from the tidal stream atlas or the diamond, referenced to HW at the named port — never guess it from the tide table.

cards.q: Why should you plan a passage around the tidal stream and not just the wind?
cards.a: Because 2 knots of stream on a 5 knot boat is 40% of your speed: fair tide gives 7 knots over the ground, foul gives 3. Over a six-hour tide that is the difference between arriving and not.

cards.q: How do you work out the total tidal effect over a three-hour passage?
cards.a: Take the set and rate for each of the three hours from the diamonds or atlas, and either plot them end to end as three successive vectors or resolve them into one resultant vector for the whole period. Then use that resultant in the course-to-steer triangle.

cards.q: What is the practical difference between working out a course to steer hour by hour and for the whole passage?
cards.a: Hour by hour keeps you close to the intended track throughout, which matters if there are dangers either side. A single resultant for the whole leg gets you to the destination but lets you wander well off the straight line in between — fine in open water, wrong in confined water.

cards.q: Why does a strong tidal stream matter when you pick up a mooring or come alongside?
cards.a: Because the boat steers by water flow, not ground speed. Approach into the stronger of wind and tide so you have steerage way at a low speed over the ground, and remember you will stop much faster with the tide against you than with it behind you.

cards.q: What is a port hand mark in IALA Region A?
cards.a: Red, can (cylindrical) shape, with a red can topmark if any, showing a red light of any rhythm except Fl(2+1)R, which is reserved for the preferred-channel mark — for example Fl R 5s. Keep it to port when travelling in the direction of buoyage.

cards.q: What is a starboard hand mark in IALA Region A?
cards.a: Green, conical shape, with a green cone topmark point up if any, showing a green light of any rhythm except Fl(2+1)G, which is reserved for the preferred-channel mark — for example Fl G 3s. Keep it to starboard in the direction of buoyage.

cards.q: What is the direction of buoyage?
cards.a: The direction a vessel takes when approaching a harbour, river or estuary from seaward, or elsewhere the direction shown on the chart by a broad arrow symbol. The general convention is clockwise around continental land masses. Around the British Isles it runs north up the west coast and through the Irish Sea, east through the English Channel, and north through the North Sea — so it is not a clockwise circuit of the islands.

cards.q: How do the lateral colours differ between IALA Region A and Region B?
cards.a: The colours are reversed: in Region B (the Americas, Japan, Korea, the Philippines) port hand is green and starboard hand is red. Shapes and topmarks are unchanged. 'Red right returning' is a Region B rule and is wrong in the UK.

cards.q: Describe a preferred channel to starboard mark in Region A.
cards.a: Red with a single broad green horizontal band, can shape, light Fl(2+1) R. It marks a channel division; treat it as a port hand mark for the main channel, which lies to starboard of it.

cards.q: Describe a preferred channel to port mark in Region A.
cards.a: Green with a single broad red horizontal band, conical shape, light Fl(2+1) G. Treat it as a starboard hand mark; the main channel lies to port of it.

cards.q: Describe the North cardinal mark.
cards.a: Black above yellow. Topmark: two black cones both pointing up. Light: Q or VQ, white. Pass to the north of it — safe water lies north of the mark.

cards.q: Describe the East cardinal mark.
cards.a: Black, yellow band, black. Topmark: two black cones base to base. Light: Q(3) 10s or VQ(3) 5s, white. Pass to the east of it.

cards.q: Describe the South cardinal mark.
cards.a: Yellow above black. Topmark: two black cones both pointing down. Light: Q(6) + LFl 15s or VQ(6) + LFl 10s, white — the long flash confirms you counted six. Pass to the south of it.

cards.q: Describe the West cardinal mark.
cards.a: Yellow, black band, yellow. Topmark: two black cones point to point, like a wine glass. Light: Q(9) 15s or VQ(9) 10s, white. Pass to the west of it.

cards.q: What is the memory aid for cardinal light rhythms?
cards.a:
A clock face: East is 3 o'clock so 3 flashes;
South is 6 o'clock so 6 flashes plus a long flash;
West is 9 o'clock so 9 flashes;
North is 12 o'clock so continuous quick flashing.

cards.q: What are the cardinal quadrant boundaries?
cards.a: NW, NE, SE and SW — true bearings 315°, 045°, 135° and 225°, measured from the danger.

cards.q: Describe an isolated danger mark.
cards.a: Black with one or more broad red horizontal bands, topmark two black spheres in a vertical line, light Fl(2) white. It is moored on or above a small isolated danger that has navigable water all round it.

cards.q: Describe a safe water mark.
cards.a:
Red and white vertical stripes,
spherical or with a single red sphere topmark,
light white: Iso, Oc, LFl 10s or Mo(A). There is navigable water all round it. Often used as a mid-channel or landfall mark.

cards.q: Describe a special mark.
cards.a:
Yellow,
any shape not conflicting with a navigational mark,
topmark a single yellow X,
light yellow, in any rhythm except those used for the white lights of cardinal, isolated danger and safe water marks. It marks a special area or feature —
spoil ground,
outfall,
cables,
military exercise area,
recreation zone,
racing marks,
ODAS buoys.

cards.q: Describe the emergency wreck marking buoy.
cards.a: Blue and yellow vertical stripes, topmark a yellow upright cross, light alternating blue and yellow, Al Oc BuY 3s. It is deployed on a newly discovered wreck until the wreck is charted and permanently marked.

cards.q: What is the difference between an isolated danger mark and a safe water mark in practice?
cards.a: The isolated danger mark sits on the hazard — never pass close to it. The safe water mark has deep water all round and may be passed on either side.

cards.q: What does a yellow buoy with a yellow X topmark near an outfall tell you?
cards.a: It is a special mark: not a navigational hazard mark in itself, but there is something there — a pipeline, cable or restricted area. Look it up on the chart before you cut inside it.

cards.q: How is a small-craft channel or a recommended track for yachts often marked?
cards.a: By small buoys, sometimes yellow special marks, or by charted small-craft channels outside the main fairway. Harbour byelaws often require small craft to use them and to keep clear of the deep-water channel.

cards.q: What is a withy or a perch?
cards.a: A local, unofficial or simple mark — a bundle of twigs or a pole — used in creeks and shallow channels. They may follow local convention rather than IALA and are not always charted, so treat them with care and read the pilot book.

cards.q: How can you tell a lit buoy from an unlit one on the chart?
cards.a: A lit buoy carries a magenta flare symbol and the light's characteristic, e.g. 'Fl G 5s'. No flare means unlit — which matters enormously if you plan to arrive after dark.

cards.q: You see a buoy with a black body, a red band and two black spheres. What is it and what do you do?
cards.a: An isolated danger mark: there is a hazard right there with navigable water round it. Identify it on the chart, work out which side gives you the room you need, and give it a wide berth.

cards.q: Which lights and marks does the IALA buoyage system NOT apply to?
cards.a:
Landfall lights,
leading lights and marks,
sector lights,
and major floating lights. They keep their own charted characteristics — so a red light in an approach is not necessarily a port-hand buoy.

cards.q: What is a 'new danger', and how is it marked?
cards.a: An uncharted hazard — wreck, rock or shoal — not yet promulgated in nautical publications. It is marked with lateral, cardinal or isolated danger marks, or with an emergency wreck marking buoy. One of the marks may be duplicated until the danger is charted, and it may carry a racon showing Morse D and an AIS transponder.

cards.q: In Region B, what is a green buoy with a red band showing Fl(2+1) G?
cards.a: A preferred channel to starboard mark. In Region B green is the port-hand colour, so the preferred-channel colours and rhythms swap over: Fl(2+1)G marks a preferred channel to starboard and Fl(2+1)R a preferred channel to port.

cards.q: What are the standard buoy shapes, and when does shape tell you nothing?
cards.a:
Can (cylindrical),
conical,
spherical,
pillar
and spar. On pillar and spar buoys — and on all fixed beacons — only the topmark and colour have navigational significance, because the body shape is dictated by the structure.

cards.q: Apart from which side to pass, what else can a cardinal mark be telling you?
cards.a:
Where the best navigable water lies;
the safe side on which to pass a danger;
or a feature in a channel — a bend, a junction, a branch, or the end of a shoal.

cards.q: What does F mean on a chart?
cards.a: Fixed — a continuous, steady light that does not change.

cards.q: What does Fl mean, and what is the pattern?
cards.a: Flashing — a single flash at regular intervals, where the duration of light is shorter than the duration of dark. Fl 5s = one flash every 5 seconds.

cards.q: What does Fl(3) 15s mean?
cards.a: Group flashing — a group of three flashes, the whole pattern repeating every 15 seconds.

cards.q: What does LFl mean?
cards.a: Long flashing — a single flash of 2 seconds or more, repeated. LFl 10s = one long flash every 10 seconds.

cards.q: What does Oc mean, and how do you recognise it?
cards.a: Occulting — the light is longer than the dark: a steady light briefly eclipsed. Oc(2) 7s = two eclipses in a 7-second period.

cards.q: What does Iso mean?
cards.a: Isophase — the periods of light and dark are exactly equal.

cards.q: What do Q and VQ mean?
cards.a:
Q quick flashing, 50-79 flashes per minute.
VQ very quick flashing, 80-159 per minute. (UQ, ultra quick, is 160 or more.)

cards.q: What does Mo(A) mean, and where would you see it?
cards.a: Morse code letter A — a short flash followed by a long flash. Commonly used on safe water marks and landfall buoys.

cards.q: What does Al mean?
cards.a: Alternating — the light shows different colours in succession from the same position, e.g. Al WR.

cards.q: What is the 'period' of a light?
cards.a: The time taken for one complete cycle of the light's pattern, from the start of one group to the start of the next. It is the number of seconds printed after the rhythm, and it is what you actually time with a watch to identify a light.

cards.q: Decode: Fl(2)WRG 10s 15m 11-8M.
cards.a:
Two flashes every 10 seconds;
the light shows white, red and green sectors;
its elevation is 15 m above the chart height datum, which is MHWS on UK charts;
and the nominal ranges are white 11 M, green 8 M, red between the two — the first figure is always white and the last green.

cards.q: Decode: Oc(2)R 7s 9m 6M.
cards.a: An occulting red light, two eclipses in a 7-second period, 9 metres above MHWS, nominal range 6 miles.

cards.q: Decode: Q(9) 15s.
cards.a: Nine quick flashes every 15 seconds — a West cardinal mark.

cards.q: Decode: Fl(2+1) R 10s.
cards.a: A group of two flashes then a single flash, red, every 10 seconds — a preferred channel to starboard mark in Region A.

cards.q: If a light shows no colour letter, what colour is it?
cards.a:
White. Colours are lettered only when they are not white: R red,
G green,
Y yellow,
Bu blue,
Vi violet,
Or orange.

cards.q: How do you positively identify a light at night?
cards.a: Time the full period with a watch, count the flashes in a group, note the colour, and compare all three with the chart or light list. Then check the bearing is consistent with your expected position. Never identify a light on colour alone.

cards.q: What is a lighthouse's 'racon' marking on the chart?
cards.a: A radar transponder beacon: it paints a Morse identification letter on a radar display outward from its position, giving a range and bearing. Charted as 'Racon(T)' or similar.

cards.q: What does IQ mean?
cards.a: Interrupted quick flashing — continuous quick flashing with a regular eclipse. IVQ and IUQ are the very quick and ultra quick equivalents.

cards.q: What does FFl mean?
cards.a: Fixed and flashing — a steady light with a brighter flash superimposed at regular intervals.

cards.q: On an Admiralty chart, what is a light's elevation measured from, and what does its charted range mean?
cards.a:
Elevation is the height of the focal plane above the chart's height datum — MHWS on UK charts — not above the sea level at the time.
Charted ranges are nominal ranges in sea miles: the luminous range in a meteorological visibility of 10 sea miles.

cards.q: A light is charted 'Fl WRG 5s 12m 11-8M'. What is the range of each colour?
cards.a: White 11 M, green 8 M, red between the two. The first figure is always white and the last is green; intermediate colours lie between.

cards.q: For a sector light or a leading line, which way are the charted bearings measured?
cards.a: Always from seaward, towards the light. To use one as a course to steer inbound you read it straight off the chart; to leave on it you use the reciprocal.

cards.q: What is the Beaufort scale, and what are forces 4, 6 and 8 called?
cards.a:
A scale of wind force from 0 to 12 based on observed sea state. Force 4 is a moderate breeze, 11-16 knots;
force 6 a strong breeze, 22-27 knots;
force 8 a gale, 34-40 knots.

cards.q: What are the wind speeds for Beaufort forces 5, 7 and 9?
cards.a:
Force 5 fresh breeze 17-21 kn;
force 7 near gale 28-33 kn;
force 9 strong gale 41-47 kn — which is the name on the Beaufort scale, though gale warnings and the shipping forecast call it severe gale 9.

cards.q: At what force do you expect to see 'many white horses' and think about the first reef?
cards.a: Force 5, a fresh breeze of 17-21 knots: moderate waves, many white horses, some spray. Most cruising yachts want the first reef in at the top of force 4 or in force 5.

cards.q: What do the shipping forecast terms 'gale', 'severe gale', 'storm' and 'violent storm' mean?
cards.a:
Gale — mean wind force 8, or gusts of 43-51 kn.
Severe gale — force 9, or gusts 52-60 kn.
Storm — force 10, or gusts 61-68 kn.
Violent storm — force 11, or gusts of 69 kn or more.

cards.q: What do 'imminent', 'soon' and 'later' mean in a shipping forecast gale warning?
cards.a:
Imminent — within 6 hours of the time of issue.
Soon — 6 to 12 hours.
Later — more than 12 hours.

cards.q: Define the marine visibility terms good, moderate, poor and very poor.
cards.a:
Good — more than 5 nautical miles.
Moderate — 2 to 5 M.
Poor — 1,000 m to 2 M.
Very poor — less than 1,000 m.
Fog is a term in the weather element rather than a visibility band, and fog means visibility below 1,000 m.

cards.q: Define the pressure-tendency terms used in the shipping forecast.
cards.a:
Change in the 3 hours before the observation, in hPa (1 hPa = 1 mb): rising or falling slowly 0.1-1.5;
rising or falling 1.6-3.5;
rising or falling quickly 3.6-6.0;
rising or falling very rapidly more than 6.0. Also rising or falling more slowly, meaning the rate is easing, and now rising or now falling, meaning it has just turned. Steady means no appreciable change.

cards.q: What do 'backing' and 'veering' mean?
cards.a:
Backing — the wind direction changes anticlockwise, e.g. SW to S.
Veering — it changes clockwise, e.g. SW to NW. In the northern hemisphere the wind veers as each front passes.

cards.q: Which direction is a wind named for?
cards.a: The direction it blows from. A westerly wind blows from the west. A tidal stream, by contrast, is named for the direction it flows towards.

cards.q: What are the parts of the shipping forecast, in order?
cards.a:
Gale warnings;
the general synopsis, meaning where the pressure systems are and where they are going;
then for each sea area in turn: wind direction and force, sea state, weather, visibility.
Then reports from coastal stations, and on some broadcasts the inshore waters forecast. It is issued four times a day and covers 24 hours.

cards.q: Where can you get a marine forecast at sea?
cards.a:
Met Office shipping and inshore waters forecasts on BBC Radio 4 FM, DAB and BBC Sounds — the 198 kHz long wave transmission closed on 27 June 2026;
Maritime Safety Information broadcasts by HM Coastguard on VHF (announced on Ch 16, given on a working channel);
NAVTEX on 518 kHz;
the Met Office and other websites and apps by mobile data;
harbour offices and marina noticeboards;
and barometer plus your own eyes.

cards.q: How does a depression behave in the northern hemisphere?
cards.a: Pressure is lowest at the centre, wind circulates anticlockwise and blows slightly inwards across the isobars, and the system usually tracks east or north-east. Closely spaced isobars mean strong wind.

cards.q: How does an anticyclone behave in the northern hemisphere?
cards.a: High pressure with clockwise circulation and light winds, widely spaced isobars, settled weather. In summer it brings fine weather and sea breezes; in winter it can bring fog, low cloud and frost. Anticyclones move slowly and block depressions.

cards.q: State Buys Ballot's law.
cards.a: In the northern hemisphere, if you stand with your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left. It lets you place the depression without a chart.

cards.q: What is a warm front and what weather does it bring?
cards.a:
The boundary where warm air rides up over cold air. Ahead of it:
high cirrus thickening to altostratus and then low, thick cloud,
pressure falling steadily,
a long spell of continuous rain,
and the wind increasing — backing as the depression first approaches, then veering through the frontal zone. As the front passes the rain eases to drizzle, the wind veers, pressure steadies and the temperature rises.

cards.q: What is a cold front and what weather does it bring?
cards.a:
Cold air undercutting warm air, giving a sharp, often squally transition:
towering cumulonimbus,
heavy showers or thunder,
a marked veer and gusting of the wind,
a sharp rise in pressure and a drop in temperature. Behind it the air is clear, bright and showery with good visibility.

cards.q: What is the warm sector like?
cards.a:
The area between the warm and cold fronts:
overcast with low stratus,
drizzle,
mild and muggy,
poor visibility and often sea fog,
with steady pressure and a steady wind direction.

cards.q: What is an occlusion?
cards.a: Where the cold front catches up with the warm front and lifts the warm sector clear of the surface. You get the cloud and rain of both fronts combined, but without the clear temperature change — a wet, murky passage of weather.

cards.q: What is the classic sequence of wind and pressure as a depression passes to your north?
cards.a:
Starting from a south-westerly gradient wind: as the depression approaches from the west the wind backs to SE and freshens while pressure falls;
the warm front passes and the wind veers to SW, pressure steadies and visibility worsens;
the cold front passes and the wind veers sharply to NW and gusts, pressure rises and visibility clears. At each front the wind veers.

cards.q: What is a trough and a ridge?
cards.a:
A trough is an elongated area of low pressure — expect a wind shift, cloud and showers even without a named front.
A ridge is an elongated area of high pressure, bringing a temporary improvement.

cards.q: What is a sea breeze, and when should you expect one?
cards.a:
On a sunny day the land heats faster than the sea, air rises over the land and cooler sea air flows in. It typically starts late morning,
blows onshore,
can reach force 4-5 by mid-afternoon and dies in the evening. It needs a sunny day and a light background wind, and it can reinforce or cancel the gradient wind.

cards.q: What is a land breeze?
cards.a: The night-time reverse: the land cools faster than the sea, so a light offshore breeze flows from land to sea in the early hours. It is usually weaker than the sea breeze.

cards.q: What is advection fog (sea fog) and why does it matter to a yacht?
cards.a: Warm, moist air moving over a colder sea surface is cooled below its dew point. It can form in a good breeze, persist for days, and it is the fog that catches yachts out in spring and early summer in the Channel — thickest often in the warm sector of a depression.

cards.q: What is radiation fog?
cards.a: Fog formed overnight over land by radiative cooling under clear skies with light winds. It drifts out of estuaries and harbour entrances at dawn and usually burns off during the morning.

cards.q: How does the barometer help you if you have no forecast?
cards.a: The trend matters more than the value. Falling steadily means a depression approaching: wind and rain. Falling quickly, 3.6-6.0 hPa in 3 hours, or very rapidly, more than 6.0 hPa in 3 hours, means a vigorous system and possibly gale-force wind. Rising means improvement, though a sharp rise behind a cold front comes with squalls.

cards.q: What clouds warn you of a squall or thunderstorm?
cards.a:
Cumulonimbus — tall, dark, anvil-topped. Expect a sudden violent wind shift and increase,
heavy rain or hail,
and a rapid drop in visibility. Reef before it arrives and get the crew clipped on.

cards.q: What is a katabatic wind and where might you meet one?
cards.a: Cold dense air draining down a slope at night, producing a strong offshore gust that arrives without warning in a sheltered-looking anchorage under high ground — common in the Mediterranean, Norway and steep-sided lochs.

cards.q: How does the wind behave near a headland or a cliff?
cards.a: It accelerates and bends round headlands, giving a stronger gust and a wind shift; under a cliff there may be a wind shadow, and then violent downdraughts and gusts a few boat lengths further out. Never assume the wind close inshore is the forecast wind.

cards.q: What does 'fog patches' or 'occasionally poor' mean in an inshore waters forecast?
cards.a: It is a qualifier, not a promise: the poor visibility or fog is expected for part of the period only, and not everywhere in the area. The Met Office publishes no numerical definition of 'occasional' or 'patches'. Plan as if you will get it, and know where you can go if it closes in.

cards.q: What is the difference between the shipping forecast and the inshore waters forecast?
cards.a: The shipping forecast covers the large sea areas offshore with mean winds and a 24-hour outlook. The inshore waters forecast covers up to 12 miles off the coast in more relevant detail — wind, weather, visibility, sea state — and is the one a Day Skipper should be using.

cards.q: What sea state terms are used, and what do they mean?
cards.a:
Calm (glassy) 0 m;
calm (rippled) 0-0.1 m;
smooth 0.1-0.5 m;
slight 0.5-1.25 m;
moderate 1.25-2.5 m;
rough 2.5-4 m;
very rough 4-6 m;
high 6-9 m;
very high 9-14 m;
phenomenal more than 14 m. These are significant wave heights — individual waves can be substantially higher.

cards.q: How should the forecast affect your go / no-go decision?
cards.a: Compare the forecast wind and sea with the limits of the boat, the crew (the least experienced person aboard) and the passage, including wind against tide, the exposure of the route and the state of the bar or entrance on arrival. If the answer is marginal for any of the three, do not go.

cards.q: What are Beaufort forces 0 to 3?
cards.a:
Force 0 calm, under 1 kn;
force 1 light air, 1-3 kn;
force 2 light breeze, 4-6 kn;
force 3 gentle breeze, 7-10 kn.

cards.q: What are Beaufort forces 10, 11 and 12?
cards.a:
Force 10 storm, 48-55 kn;
force 11 violent storm, 56-63 kn;
force 12 hurricane force, 64 kn or more.

cards.q: What does 'hurricane force' mean in a forecast, and why not just 'hurricane'?
cards.a: Winds of force 12, 64 knots or more. The Met Office says hurricane force because hurricane on its own means a true tropical cyclone, which is not experienced in British waters.

cards.q: What is a strong wind warning, and why does it matter more to you than a gale warning?
cards.a: A warning of winds of force 6 or more in inshore waters. It is issued well below gale force, and force 6 is the threshold at which most small craft should think again — so it is the warning a Day Skipper should act on.

cards.q: What do 'slowly', 'steadily', 'rather quickly', 'rapidly' and 'very rapidly' mean about a pressure system?
cards.a:
How fast the system is moving: slowly under 15 kn;
steadily 15-25 kn;
rather quickly 25-35 kn;
rapidly 35-45 kn;
very rapidly more than 45 kn. Do not confuse these with the pressure-tendency terms, which describe how fast the barometer is changing.

cards.q: What does 'becoming cyclonic' mean in a forecast?
cards.a: There will be a considerable change of wind direction across the path of a depression within that area — a low is passing through, so expect the wind to swing right round rather than settle.

cards.q: What is in the coastal station reports, and what are they for?
cards.a:
Actual observations, not forecasts:
wind direction and force,
visibility,
sea-level pressure and pressure tendency. Use them to check the forecast against reality, and to see where the system has actually got to.

cards.q: How much stronger than the mean wind are the gusts, and what should you plan for?
cards.a: Typically 40 to 60% above the mean — one to two Beaufort forces. A forecast force 6 can gust force 8, which is why warnings quote gust bands. Reef for the gusts, not the mean.

cards.q: How can you anticipate sea fog before you sail?
cards.a: Compare the forecast dew point with the sea temperature: if the air's dew point is at or above the sea temperature, warm moist air moving over the colder sea will fog. Classic on south-westerly winds in the Channel in spring and early summer — and it does not need a calm.

cards.q: What is the difference between navigation and pilotage?
cards.a: Navigation is getting from A to B in open water using the chart, the tide and the compass, with time to plot. Pilotage is close-quarters work near the shore where there is no time to plot: you work from a prepared plan, marks, transits, depths and eyeball.

cards.q: What goes into a pilotage plan?
cards.a:
A simple sketch you can read one-handed in the dark:
the legs with courses and distances,
the buoys and lights in the order you will see them with their characteristics,
transits and leading lines,
clearing bearings for each hazard,
a depth contour to stay outside,
the tidal height needed and when,
waypoints,
and an abort plan.

cards.q: Why is a transit better than a compass bearing?
cards.a: It has no error at all — no variation, no deviation, no reading error — and it shows you instantly whether you are drifting off the line. Two charted objects in line is the most reliable pilotage tool there is.

cards.q: What is a leading line?
cards.a: A charted line, usually defined by two marks or two lights in transit, that leads safely into a harbour or through a channel. The chart gives its bearing; the marks give you the accuracy.

cards.q: What is a clearing bearing and how do you use it?
cards.a: A bearing of a charted object which, if you keep the actual bearing greater than (or less than) it, keeps you clear of a danger. Written as 'keep the bearing of the church spire greater than 070°', or NLT / NMT on the chart — a single number the helm can hold without looking at the chart.

cards.q: How do you use the echo sounder as a safety line?
cards.a: Choose a depth contour that clears the dangers, work out what the sounder should read at that contour for the height of tide at the time, and treat that number as a wall: if the depth falls to it, turn away. It works in fog and at night.

cards.q: What is a head bearing, and what is it good for?
cards.a: The bearing of a mark you are heading towards. Watch it: if it stays constant you are making good the track towards the mark; if it changes, the tide is setting you off and you must alter.

cards.q: What is the practical rule about speed in pilotage?
cards.a: Go slowly enough that you can keep ahead of the boat. If you cannot identify the next mark before you reach the last one, slow down, stop, or turn back onto a reciprocal course until you have sorted out where you are.

cards.q: What preparation should be done on deck before entering a harbour?
cards.a:
Fenders and warps rigged both sides,
boat hook to hand,
anchor ready to let go,
sails stowed or ready to drop,
engine warm and tested in ahead and astern,
crew briefed with jobs allocated,
and the pilotage plan and VHF channel to hand in the cockpit.

cards.q: Why brief the crew before the entrance rather than during it?
cards.a:
Because once you are in it you will be busy with the helm and the marks, and a shouted instruction in a confined channel is how boats get damaged. Allocate helm,
lookout,
fenders,
lines and log-keeper in advance.

cards.q: What information do you look up before entering an unfamiliar harbour?
cards.a:
Approach and entrance in the pilot book and almanac,
harbour plan,
tidal height and stream at your arrival time,
any bar, sill or lock and its operating hours,
port signals and traffic lights,
VHF working channel and whether you must call in,
visitor berths,
prohibited areas,
and the abort options if you cannot get in.

cards.q: What do port entry traffic signals typically mean?
cards.a:
Three flashing red lights in a vertical line = serious emergency, all vessels stop or divert as instructed (IPTS 1).
Three fixed reds = vessels shall not proceed (IPTS 2).
Red, white, red = do not proceed except outside the main channel (IPTS 3).
Three greens = proceed, one-way traffic;
green, white, green = proceed, two-way traffic. Local variations exist, so read the almanac entry for the specific port before you rely on it.

cards.q: What is 'IPTS'?
cards.a: The International Port Traffic Signals, a standardised set of light signals controlling movement in and out of harbours, described in the almanac. A single yellow light alongside the main signal often exempts small craft — but only where the port says so.

cards.q: How do you handle pilotage at night?
cards.a:
Prepare everything in daylight,
preserve night vision with red light and no white deck lights,
identify each light by counting its period rather than guessing,
use the order of lights in your plan,
post a dedicated lookout free of other tasks,
and go slower than you would by day. Background shore lights make buoys very hard to pick out.

cards.q: Why are lit buoys so hard to spot on the approach to a lit town?
cards.a:
Because a 3-mile flashing buoy competes with streetlights, illuminated signs and moving car headlights ashore. Use transits,
leading lights,
depth and your prepared bearings, not just buoy-hopping.

cards.q: What is an abort plan and when do you decide to use it?
cards.a:
The pre-agreed route back out to safe water, with the course to steer and the depth you expect. Decide the trigger in advance —
cannot identify the leading marks,
too much wind across the entrance,
not enough depth,
traffic in the channel
— and act on it early rather than pressing on.

cards.q: How does the tidal stream inside a harbour entrance differ from outside?
cards.a: It can reverse, accelerate through the gap, and set strongly across the entrance or along a pontoon face. Expect an eddy behind a breakwater running the opposite way to the main stream, and plan the last hundred metres for it.

cards.q: What actions do you take when fog closes in?
cards.a:
Fix your position immediately while you still can.
Slow to a safe speed, engine on and ready.
Sound the fog signal.
Show navigation lights.
Lifejackets on and crew on deck as extra lookouts, listening as well as looking.
Hoist the radar reflector.
Get out of shipping lanes and busy channels.
Plot continuously and consider anchoring in shallow water clear of the fairway.

cards.q: Which rule governs your conduct in fog, and what is different about it?
cards.a: Rule 19. It applies when vessels are not in sight of one another in or near restricted visibility, and there is no stand-on vessel — every vessel has an obligation to avoid collision.

cards.q: Why is it safer to be in shallow water in fog?
cards.a: Because commercial traffic cannot follow you there. Getting outside the buoyed channel into water too shallow for shipping, or anchoring there, removes the biggest single threat.

cards.q: Why anchor rather than keep moving in thick fog?
cards.a:
An anchored boat is not closing anything,
is easier to fix,
sounds a distinctive signal,
and lets you listen properly. Anchor clear of the channel,
sound the bell signal,
and keep a lookout.

cards.q: What should you listen for in fog, and how reliable is it?
cards.a:
Fog signals,
engine noise,
breaking water on a shore,
and bell buoys. Sound in fog is deceptive: it can be deflected, reflected and blanketed, so a signal can seem to come from the wrong direction or be inaudible in a 'shadow'. Never bet your position on hearing alone.

cards.q: How useful is a small-craft radar reflector in practice?
cards.a: Better than nothing, but a yacht is a poor radar target, especially heeled or in a rough sea where sea clutter hides her. Assume you have not been seen and keep out of the way.

cards.q: What is AIS and how does it help in poor visibility?
cards.a: The Automatic Identification System broadcasts a vessel's identity, position, course and speed over VHF. A receiver shows you shipping with its CPA and TCPA. An AIS transponder makes you visible to them too. It does not show vessels without AIS, and small craft often carry none.

cards.q: What is CPA and TCPA?
cards.a:
Closest Point of Approach — how near the other vessel will pass if nothing changes.
Time to CPA — how long until that happens. They are the two numbers that tell you whether you have a problem and how long you have to solve it.

cards.q: What are the fog signals you are most likely to hear from a big ship, and what do they mean?
cards.a:
One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes — a power-driven vessel making way.
Two prolonged blasts about 2 seconds apart — a power-driven vessel underway but stopped.
One prolonged and two short — a sailing vessel, or a vessel fishing, towing or pushing, not under command, restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, or constrained by draught. All at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.

cards.q: Should you use the engine in fog if you are under sail?
cards.a: Usually yes: it gives you manoeuvrability and the ability to stop, which Rule 19 expects. But turn it off periodically, or have a crew member well forward, so you can listen. Remember that once under power you must show the correct lights, hoist the black cone, point down, forward by day, and that your fog signal changes from one prolonged and two short to one prolonged.

cards.q: What is the greatest danger to a yacht in fog in the Channel?
cards.a: Being run down by shipping that cannot see you and may not detect you on radar, especially in or near a traffic separation scheme or the approaches to a major port. Cross the lanes at right angles, quickly, and preferably not in fog at all.

cards.q: What are the immediate actions for a man overboard?
cards.a:
Shout 'man overboard' to get everyone on deck;
throw buoyancy — danbuoy and lifebuoy — immediately;
detail one person to point at the casualty and do nothing else;
press the MOB button on the plotter or GNSS;
start the engine, checking for lines over the side;
and manoeuvre back to the casualty.

cards.q: Describe the reach-tack-reach MOB recovery under sail.
cards.a:
Get onto a beam reach — bearing away if you were beating, luffing up if you were running — and sail on for four to six boat lengths.
Tack, never gybe.
Come onto the reciprocal beam reach, bear away enough to get to leeward of the casualty, then turn up and approach on a close reach, controlling speed by easing the sails.
Stop with the casualty alongside on the leeward side at or just forward of the shrouds, engine out of gear — never ahead of the bow, where you lose sight of them.

cards.q: Describe the crash-stop (heave-to) MOB recovery.
cards.a: Tack immediately without touching the headsail sheet, so the headsail is left backed. The boat stops quickly and stays near the casualty. Then drop or furl the headsail and motor or sail the last few lengths. Its virtue is that you never get far from the casualty. Note that the American Quick Stop is a different manoeuvre: you keep turning through a gybe and circle back.

cards.q: Why do you approach a man overboard from downwind, and stop with them to leeward?
cards.a: Approaching from downwind on a close reach lets you spill the sails to control speed and stop. Recover on the leeward side because a yacht blows downwind far faster than a person in the water, so a casualty left to windward is one you drift away from; the hull also gives them a lee, and the heeled leeward rail is the lowest freeboard. Stop the boat and take the engine out of gear before they are anywhere near the hull.

cards.q: Why should the engine be out of gear before anyone comes alongside the hull?
cards.a: Because the propeller will kill or maim someone in the water. Neutral, and preferably stopped, before the casualty is anywhere near the stern or the boarding ladder.

cards.q: Why lift a MOB casualty horizontally if you can?
cards.a: Because prolonged immersion causes the blood to pool in the legs. Lifting vertically can drop the blood pressure and cause post-immersion collapse and cardiac arrest. Keep them horizontal during and after recovery, and handle them gently.

cards.q: How can you get a casualty back on board a yacht?
cards.a:
A boarding ladder if they can climb;
a lifting strop or MOB recovery sling on a spare halyard led to a winch;
the mainsail or a sail used as a scoop under them;
a bight of rope as a step;
or the dinghy. Practise it — a wet, cold adult in oilskins is an extraordinarily heavy lift.

cards.q: When would you send a MAYDAY for a man overboard?
cards.a: As soon as you lose sight of the casualty, or if you are short-handed, or if the first recovery attempt fails, or if there is any injury. It is far better to cancel a MAYDAY than to send it too late.

cards.q: What is a MAYDAY and how do you send one?
cards.a:
The distress signal for grave and imminent danger. Press and hold the DSC distress button for 5 seconds first, then on Ch 16:
MAYDAY ×3,
'THIS IS' + vessel name ×3,
MMSI and callsign,
then MAYDAY + name + MMSI,
position,
nature of distress,
assistance required,
number of people on board,
any other useful information,
OVER.

cards.q: What is a PAN-PAN used for?
cards.a:
Urgency: a very urgent message about the safety of the vessel or a person, where there is not grave and imminent danger —
engine failure in a safe position,
a broken bone,
a dismasting with no injury,
or a request for medical advice.

cards.q: What is a SÉCURITÉ message?
cards.a: A safety message: a navigational or meteorological warning. The Coastguard uses it to broadcast gale warnings and hazards; you would use it to report a container adrift or an unlit obstruction.

cards.q: What is a MAYDAY RELAY?
cards.a: A distress message passed on behalf of another vessel that cannot transmit its own, or whose distress you have witnessed. You broadcast 'MAYDAY RELAY' three times, then 'THIS IS' your own vessel, and pass on the details.

cards.q: What are SEELONCE MAYDAY and SEELONCE FEENEE?
cards.a: SEELONCE MAYDAY imposes radio silence on Ch 16 so distress traffic can be heard; it is normally sent by the station controlling the distress. SEELONCE FEENEE ends the silence and returns the channel to normal working.

cards.q: What is Ch 16 for, and what is Ch 70?
cards.a: Ch 16 is the distress, safety and calling channel, monitored by the Coastguard — keep a listening watch on it. Ch 70 carries DSC data only: never transmit voice on it.

cards.q: What is DSC and what does a distress alert send?
cards.a: Digital Selective Calling: a data burst on Ch 70 containing your MMSI number, the nature of distress if you have time to select it, and your GNSS position and time. It is received automatically by the Coastguard and by DSC-equipped vessels nearby. Always follow it with a voice MAYDAY on Ch 16.

cards.q: What qualification do you need to operate a marine VHF, and what is an MMSI?
cards.a: The Short Range Certificate (SRC), and the vessel needs a Ship Radio Licence. The MMSI is the nine-digit Maritime Mobile Service Identity that identifies your station in DSC calls — it must be programmed correctly and registered.

cards.q: List the recognised distress signals.
cards.a:
Continuous sounding of a fog-signal apparatus;
a gun or explosive signal at about 1-minute intervals;
rockets or shells throwing red stars fired one at a time at short intervals;
red parachute or hand flare;
orange smoke;
SOS by any means;
the spoken word 'MAYDAY';
code flags NC;
a square flag with a ball above or below;
flames on the vessel;
slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering outstretched arms;
a DSC alert;
EPIRB, PLB or SART.

cards.q: What do you do if you are taking on water?
cards.a:
Get the crew into lifejackets and send a distress or urgency call early.
Find the source — seacocks, hoses, stern gland, log impeller, keel bolts, a holed hull — and stem it with a bung, a cushion, a sail or anything you can jam and brace in place.
Run all the pumps and bail.
Head for shallow water or a beach if you cannot control it.

cards.q: What do you do if the steering fails?
cards.a:
Take the way off.
Rig the emergency tiller on the rudder stock — know where it lives before you need it.
If the rudder itself is gone, balance the sails to steer, or stream a drogue or bucket on a bridle from the quarters and adjust the lines to steer.
If you cannot manoeuvre, exhibit two all-round red lights in a vertical line, or two black balls by day, for not under command, and sound one prolonged plus two short blasts in restricted visibility.

cards.q: You run aground. What do you check first, and what changes depending on whether the tide is rising or falling?
cards.a:
Check the crew, then check for damage and water ingress.
Stop the engine if you may have fouled something or may suck in sand.
Sound round the boat with a lead line or from the dinghy to find which way the deep water lies — it is often not the way you came.
Note whether the tide is rising or falling, because that decides everything.
On a rising tide, and on a fin keel, heel her with crew weight or the boom out to reduce draught and motor or kedge off towards the deep water; heeling a bilge-keeler or long-keeler gains you little.
On a falling tide act within seconds or prepare to sit it out: lay a kedge to hold her, pad and support the side she will lie on, close the seacocks and hatches, and get the crew somewhere safe.

cards.q: What do you do if you are dismasted?
cards.a:
Secure the crew first.
Stop the engine to keep rigging out of the propeller.
Get the rig alongside and lash it, or cut it away with bolt croppers if it is holing the hull.
Recover what you can for a jury rig, motor if you can, and make a PAN-PAN or MAYDAY according to the danger.

cards.q: How do you take a tow?
cards.a:
Agree the plan on VHF first.
Use your strongest points — round a keel-stepped mast, never a deck-stepped one, or through both bow fairleads to the primary winches or a substantial cleat so the load is spread — with chafe protection.
Keep the tow long and elastic, go slowly, and have a crew member ready with a knife at the towline.
Nobody stands in line with a loaded rope.

cards.q: What do you need to know about a helicopter rescue?
cards.a:
Follow the winchman's instructions exactly and only over VHF Ch 16 or as directed.
Lower sails if told to, keep the deck clear, secure loose gear, brief the crew, do not touch the wire until it has earthed on the deck or in the water, and never make it fast to the boat.
Motor a steady course as directed, usually with the wind on a bow.

cards.q: What is the first thing you should do in almost any emergency?
cards.a: Stop, take a breath and account for your crew. Then decide whether you need outside help and call for it early — the situation will not get simpler, and rescue assets need time to reach you.

cards.q: What is the procedure for cancelling a false or resolved distress alert?
cards.a:
Do not just switch off. Transmit on Ch 16:
'All stations' ×3,
'this is' + vessel name,
MMSI and callsign,
the time,
'cancel my distress alert of [time]' and 'out'.
Tell the Coastguard what happened. An uncancelled alert sends people to sea for nothing.

cards.q: How do you recover a man overboard under power?
cards.a:
Same immediate actions — shout, throw, point, MOB button.
Then turn towards the side the casualty went over, so the stern and the propeller swing away from them.
Approach slowly into the wind and sea so the boat lies steady, aim to stop with the casualty on the leeward side at the shrouds, and put the engine in neutral, preferably stopped, before anyone is near the hull.
Never approach with the casualty ahead of the bow, where you lose sight of them.

cards.q: You have lost sight of the man overboard. What now?
cards.a:
MAYDAY immediately — do not search first and call later.
Note the MOB waypoint and the time, and work out the datum: the casualty drifts with the tidal stream plus a little leeway, and the boat drifts faster.
Return down the reciprocal of your track at slow speed with every crew member searching an allocated sector, and search across the tide.
Keep passing the position and elapsed time to the Coastguard so they can compute their own drift.

cards.q: What checks do you make before starting the engine?
cards.a:
Engine oil level,
gearbox oil,
coolant level,
raw-water seacock open,
raw-water strainer clear,
drive belt tension and condition,
fuel level and no water in the filter or bowl,
no oil or water in the bilge under the engine,
gear lever in neutral,
and nothing loose in the engine bay.

cards.q: What do you check immediately after starting?
cards.a:
That cooling water is coming out with the exhaust,
that the oil pressure and alternator warning lights have gone out,
the exhaust note and colour,
and no unusual noise, smoke or vibration. No cooling water means stop the engine at once.

cards.q: What running checks do you make on passage?
cards.a:
Temperature,
oil pressure,
battery charging,
cooling water flow,
engine note and vibration,
fuel remaining against hours run,
no smell of exhaust or fuel below,
and a look in the engine bay for drips, chafe or a loose belt.

cards.q: What checks do you make after stopping the engine?
cards.a:
Let it idle briefly before shutting down if it has been working hard, then stop it, and if the boat will be left,
close the raw-water seacock,
check for leaks,
and top up the fuel to reduce condensation. Note the hours run in the log.

cards.q: How does a diesel engine's cooling system work on a yacht?
cards.a: Almost always indirect: raw sea water is drawn in through the seacock and strainer, passed by an impeller pump through a heat exchanger and then out with the exhaust, where it also cools and silences it. Fresh water and antifreeze circulate round the engine itself.

cards.q: The engine overheats — what are the likely causes and what do you check first?
cards.a:
Loss of raw-water flow: seacock shut,
blocked strainer or intake,
weed or a plastic bag on the inlet,
a failed impeller,
or a slipping or broken belt. Also low coolant, or a blocked heat exchanger. Stop the engine, look at whether water is coming out of the exhaust, and work back from there. Do not open the fresh-water header cap while the engine is hot — scalding coolant will blow out.

cards.q: Why does the engine stop or lose power, and what do you check?
cards.a:
Almost always fuel: empty tank,
blocked pre-filter or fine filter,
water or diesel bug in the fuel,
air in the system,
a shut-off fuel cock,
or a stopped lift pump. Check the filter bowl for water and dirt, change the filter, and bleed the system.

cards.q: How do you bleed air out of a diesel fuel system?
cards.a:
Fill and refit the filters, then bleed each point in turn working from the tank towards the injectors —
pre-filter,
lift pump,
fine filter,
then the injection pump — operating the manual lift-pump lever until fuel runs out clear and bubble-free, closing each screw before moving on. If it still will not start, slacken the injector unions half a turn only and crank in bursts of no more than 10 seconds, keeping hands and face clear: fuel at injection pressure can inject through skin and cause a serious injury. Many modern engines self-bleed — check the manual first.

cards.q: Why must a diesel engine be bled, when a petrol engine need not?
cards.a: Because the injection system relies on very high pressure and cannot compress the air, so an air lock stops fuel reaching the cylinder altogether. Air gets in when the tank runs dry, a filter is changed, or a joint leaks.

cards.q: What routine maintenance does a yacht diesel need?
cards.a:
Oil and oil filter change at the manufacturer's interval,
fuel pre-filter and fine filter,
air filter,
impeller (carry a spare),
anodes in the heat exchanger,
drive belt,
coolant strength,
gearbox oil,
stern gland grease or seal check,
and battery terminals and electrolyte.

cards.q: How do you adjust the tension of the alternator drive belt, and how tight is right?
cards.a: Slacken the alternator mounting and adjusting bolts, lever the alternator out, and retighten. Correct tension gives about 10 mm of deflection at the middle of the longest run when pushed firmly with a thumb. Too loose and it slips and the water pump stops; too tight and you wreck the bearings.

cards.q: How do you estimate fuel consumption and range?
cards.a: For a small yacht diesel, a rough rule is about 1 litre per hour for every 10 hp at cruising revs; better still, measure your own by hours run against litres put in. Range = usable tank capacity / consumption per hour × speed, and never plan to use the last quarter of the tank.

cards.q: What is prop walk (paddle-wheel effect), and which way does it push?
cards.a: Paddle-wheel effect (prop walk): the propeller pushes the stern sideways, most noticeably in astern. A right-handed propeller in astern walks the stern to port. Learn which way yours goes and use it to bring the stern in when berthing.

cards.q: What is 'prop wash' and how do you use it?
cards.a: The stream of water the propeller throws over the rudder. Ahead, it gives the rudder bite, so a brief burst of ahead power with the helm over will turn the boat even at a standstill. In astern there is no prop wash over the rudder, so steering astern needs way on.

cards.q: Why should you check for lines in the water before starting the engine?
cards.a: Because a mooring line, sheet or MOB retrieval line round the propeller stops the engine, may damage the shaft and gland, and leaves you without power at the worst moment. It is the standard mistake in a man-overboard drill.

cards.q: What is a stern gland and why check it?
cards.a: The seal where the propeller shaft leaves the hull. A traditional packed gland should drip slowly when running and be greased regularly; a modern lip or face seal should not drip at all. A dry traditional gland overheats; a leaking one floods the bilge.

cards.q: What do black, blue and white exhaust smoke suggest?
cards.a:
Black — incomplete combustion: overloading, a dirty air filter, a fouled propeller or bottom.
Blue — burning lubricating oil: worn engine.
White — water vapour or unburnt fuel: a cold engine, water in the fuel, or in the worst case a head gasket.

cards.q: The starter turns the engine but it will not fire — what is your sequence?
cards.a:
Check the stop control is in, the fuel cock open and the tank has fuel;
look for water or air in the filter;
feel whether the glow plugs or cold-start aid have been used;
check the throttle is not at idle stop;
then bleed the fuel system. Do not keep cranking — you will flatten the battery and fill the exhaust with fuel.

cards.q: You have picked up a rope round the propeller. What do you do?
cards.a:
Engine into neutral and stop it at once — take the key out so nobody restarts it. Sail or anchor clear of danger. Try to unwind it from on deck with a boat hook, turning the shaft by hand if you can reach it. Only go in the water in calm, sheltered conditions,
engine stopped and key removed,
tethered,
with someone watching,
and with a mask and a serrated knife — never at sea or in a stream. Otherwise anchor or take a tow and deal with it in harbour.

cards.q: How do you change a raw-water impeller, and what else must you check?
cards.a:
Shut the raw-water seacock. Undo the pump cover plate,
keep the gasket or O-ring,
and pull the impeller out with pliers or an extractor. Fit the new one the right way round with a smear of glycerine,
refit the cover,
open the seacock,
then start up and confirm water is coming out with the exhaust. Account for every broken vane — any left in the system will be jammed in the heat exchanger and will overheat you again. Carry a spare impeller, gasket and the right spanner.

cards.q: What tools and spares should be aboard a cruising yacht?
cards.a:
Impeller and gasket,
fuel pre-filter and fine filter,
engine oil and an extractor pump,
drive belt,
gearbox oil,
jubilee clips,
self-amalgamating and duct tape,
spare fuses and bulbs,
wire and terminals,
softwood bungs,
sail-repair tape,
needle and thread,
spare shackles and blocks,
spare line,
hose clips,
bolt croppers or a hacksaw for the rigging,
spanners and sockets,
screwdrivers,
mole grips,
a sharp knife,
a torch —
and the engine manual.

cards.q: What are the two things that always determine how you approach a berth, buoy or anchorage?
cards.a: The wind and the tide, and which of the two is stronger. Approach into the stronger one so it slows you down and you keep steerage way at low speed over the ground.

cards.q: How do you come alongside a pontoon under power?
cards.a:
Assess wind and tide, and approach into the stronger of them at a shallow angle, at the slowest speed that keeps steerage. Rig fenders and lines both sides in advance,
brief the crew,
stop the boat with a burst astern,
and get a midships or bow line ashore first — then springs and the rest.

cards.q: Which line do you get ashore first when coming alongside, and why?
cards.a: A midships line, taken to a cleat abreast of or just ahead of the boat, so it both checks the boat's way and holds her in — one line and one crew member can hold a yacht alongside while you sort out the rest. Bow and stern lines and springs follow. Never send a crew member jumping ashore with a line: step off, do not leap.

cards.q: How do you leave a pontoon berth with the wind pinning you on?
cards.a:
Decide which end you want out.
Stern out: keep a bow line and a bow spring — bow led to a cleat aft of you — and motor gently ahead against it with the helm towards the pontoon; the stern swings out, then go astern out of the berth.
Bow out: keep a stern line and a stern spring — stern led to a cleat ahead of you — and motor gently astern against it with the helm towards the pontoon; the bow swings out, then drive ahead. Fender the pivot point and use slipped lines so nobody is left ashore.

cards.q: What is a slipped line, and why use one?
cards.a: A line taken round a cleat or ring ashore and back to the boat, so the crew can release it from on board without anyone going ashore. It is how you leave a berth or a buoy short-handed.

cards.q: How do you pick up a mooring buoy?
cards.a: Work out which way the boats already on the moorings are lying, approach from downwind or down-tide into the stronger of the two, aim to arrive with just enough way to stop with the buoy at the bow, and have a crew member with a boat hook and a line rigged through the bow fairlead ready to pass through the buoy's ring or pick up the pick-up buoy.

cards.q: How do you handle a boat going astern?
cards.a:
Slowly, and expect prop walk to pull the stern one way. There is no prop wash over the rudder, so you need way on before the rudder does anything. Look astern,
put the helm over gently,
and use short bursts of power rather than continuous revs.

cards.q: How do you turn a yacht in a confined space under power?
cards.a: Use a standing turn: helm hard over in the direction you want to turn, and leave it there. A short burst ahead sends prop wash over the rudder and kicks the stern round, swinging the bow. A short burst astern kills the headway — accepting that the rudder does very little astern and prop walk will dominate. Alternate short bursts and the boat pivots with almost no forward movement. Turn the way prop walk helps you, not against it.

cards.q: Why should you never use your hands or feet to fend off?
cards.a: Because a few tonnes of boat crushes fingers and legs. Use a fender or a boat hook, and if the boat is going to hit, let it hit — the gel coat is cheaper than a hand.

cards.q: How do you rig a headsail correctly?
cards.a:
Hank on or feed the luff into the foil from the tack up,
shackle the tack,
attach the halyard to the head making sure it is not twisted round the forestay,
lead both sheets outside the shrouds through the fairleads to the winches,
and put stopper knots in the ends.

cards.q: What is sail trim on the different points of sailing?
cards.a: Close hauled — sails hard in. Close reach — eased slightly. Beam reach — about half out. Broad reach — well out. Run — right out, boom well off and the headsail goosewinged or poled out. The rule is to ease until the luff just lifts, then pull in until it stops.

cards.q: What are the signs you are over-canvassed and should reef?
cards.a:
Excessive heel,
heavy weather helm,
the boat slowing and slamming rather than accelerating,
the leeward rail down,
the crew uncomfortable,
and the helm working hard to keep her on track. If you are wondering whether to reef, reef.

cards.q: How do you put a reef in with slab reefing?
cards.a:
Head up or heave to,
take up on the topping lift,
ease the kicker and the mainsheet,
drop the halyard to the mark,
hook or pull down the luff cringle at the tack,
tension the halyard,
haul in the leech reefing line to the clew,
tension the foot,
ease the topping lift and re-set the kicker,
then bear away and trim.

cards.q: How do you shake out a reef?
cards.a:
In the reverse order:
take up the topping lift,
ease the halyard slightly and the reefing line,
free the luff cringle,
then hoist the halyard fully,
re-tension the outhaul and kicker,
ease the topping lift,
and trim. Make sure the reefing line runs free so it does not tear the sail.

cards.q: How do you heave to, and why would you?
cards.a:
Tack the boat without releasing the headsail sheet so the headsail is backed, then lash the helm to leeward and ease the mainsail. The boat lies quietly at a slow drift. Use it to reef,
eat,
sort out a problem,
wait for a tide or a lock,
or make a repair.

cards.q: What is weather helm and lee helm?
cards.a:
Weather helm — the boat tries to turn up into the wind, so you hold the tiller to windward (wheel to leeward) to keep her straight; that is where the name comes from. A little is desirable; a lot means too much mainsail or too much heel.
Lee helm — she tries to turn away from the wind and you hold the tiller to leeward; it is dangerous, and usually means too much headsail or too little main.

cards.q: How does a yacht behave differently under sail when you berth or anchor?
cards.a: You cannot stop instantly and you cannot go astern, so you must plan an approach that lets you spill wind from the sails to control speed — head-to-wind or close-reaching in — with an escape route if it goes wrong. Have the anchor ready, and know where you will bear away to if you have to abort.

cards.q: What are the commands for tacking and gybing?
cards.a:
Tacking: 'Ready about?' — crew confirm — 'Lee-oh' as you put the helm down.
Gybing: 'Stand by to gybe' — check the mainsheet and kicker are in and the boom controlled — 'Gybe-oh'. In both cases the point is that everyone knows what is about to happen.

cards.q: What is an accidental gybe, and how do you avoid one?
cards.a:
The boom crashing across uncontrolled when running or on a broad reach — it can knock someone overboard or break the rig. Avoid it by not sailing dead downwind in a seaway,
rigging a preventer,
watching the wind indicator and the helm,
and briefing the crew to keep their heads down when running.

cards.q: What is a preventer and when do you rig it?
cards.a: A line from the end of the boom led forward to a strong point on the foredeck to stop the boom crossing in an accidental gybe. Rig it whenever you are running or on a broad reach, especially at night or in a swell.

cards.q: How do you handle a yacht in strong wind under power?
cards.a:
Reduce speed to keep the bow from slamming,
steer to take the seas at a slight angle rather than dead on,
expect the bow to blow off downwind at low speed,
allow much more room for every manoeuvre,
and remember you may not be able to hold a head-to-wind position at all.

cards.q: What is the effect of waves on boat handling and crew?
cards.a:
They slow the boat,
throw her off course,
make the deck dangerous
and cause seasickness and fatigue. Slowing down and altering course a few degrees to change the angle of encounter often transforms the ride, and a tired crew makes mistakes — plan watches and hot food.

cards.q: How do you rig for a lock?
cards.a: Fenders both sides, long bow and stern lines ready to loop over the bollards or a ladder rung, and one crew on each. Keep the lines slipped from on board and tend them as the water level changes — never make fast solid in a rising or falling lock.

cards.q: How do you go bow-to or stern-to a quay with a lazy line, Mediterranean style?
cards.a:
Approach slowly straight in,
drop the anchor or pick up the lazy line at the marked point,
get two stern lines ashore to the quay bollards,
then tension the lazy line or anchor cable to hold the bow off. Have a boarding plank or ladder ready, and fenders where the neighbours are.

cards.q: How do you raft up alongside another yacht?
cards.a:
Ask permission on approach.
Rig fenders high and at the widest points, and approach into the stronger of wind and tide as you would a pontoon.
Get your bow and stern lines onto the inside boat, then run your own shore lines — a bow line and a stern line to the pontoon — so your weight is not hanging on your neighbour.
Cross their foredeck, never the cockpit, and stagger the masts so the rigs cannot clash in a swell.
Agree who is leaving when.

cards.q: How do you come alongside when a tidal stream is running along the berth?
cards.a: Always approach against the stream, even if that means passing the berth and turning to come back. Head up into it at a shallow angle at the speed that gives you steerage over the ground — which can be several knots through the water while barely moving over it — and use the stream as your brake. Get the midships or upstream line ashore first. Coming alongside downstream you cannot stop, and the stream will take the bow out.

cards.q: Preparing for sea: name five things you do below decks and five on deck.
cards.a:
Below: stow everything so nothing can fly across in a knockdown,
lockers and floorboards secured,
heavy gear low and central,
washboards and hatch to hand,
gas off at the bottle,
kettle and flask filled,
seacocks checked,
bilge dry,
chart and plan at the chart table.
On deck: sail ties and halyards clear and led,
sheets rove and stoppered,
anchor secured,
warps and fenders stowed and not trailing,
dinghy and outboard lashed,
jackstays rigged,
lifebuoy and danbuoy free to release,
tender painter clear of the propeller. Then walk round and look at it all again.

cards.q: What does SOLAS Chapter V require of a small craft skipper?
cards.a:
Regulation 34 requires you to plan the passage before you go:
weather,
tides,
limitations of the vessel,
the crew,
navigational dangers,
a contingency plan,
and leaving details of your intentions with someone ashore. Chapter V also requires you to carry a radar reflector if practicable,
to know the lifesaving signals,
to assist anyone in distress at sea,
to report dangers to navigation,
and not to misuse distress signals.

cards.q: List the elements of a passage plan.
cards.a:
Weather forecast and how you will update it;
tidal heights and streams and any tidal gates;
limitations of the vessel (draught, air draught, fuel and water range, gear);
the crew's experience, fitness and hours of darkness;
navigational dangers;
a contingency plan with bolt holes;
and information ashore.

cards.q: What is a bolt hole and why does every leg need one?
cards.a: A port or anchorage you can divert to if the weather, the crew or the boat changes the plan. Identify it in advance with its approach, its tidal restrictions and the conditions in which it is usable, because you will be choosing it when you are tired and it is dark.

cards.q: What do you leave with someone ashore?
cards.a:
Your destination and route,
ETA,
the boat's name, description and sail number,
the number of people aboard,
your contact details and safety equipment,
and clear instructions on what to do — and what not to do — if you are overdue. Then tell them when you arrive.

cards.q: How do you work out an ETA for a passage leg?
cards.a: Distance divided by expected speed over the ground for each leg, allowing for the tide hour by hour and for a realistic boat speed rather than your best ever. Add contingency time, and check the arrival time against the tidal window at the destination.

cards.q: How do you plan a passage around tidal gates?
cards.a:
Work backwards from the gate. Decide the time you must be at each gate (a headland at slack water,
a bar on a rising tide,
a lock or sill within its window), then compute the departure time from the passage times between them. If the gates do not line up, the passage does not work — change the day.

cards.q: What are the limitations of the vessel that should shape a plan?
cards.a:
Draught and air draught,
fuel and water capacity and range under power,
the sail wardrobe and reefing arrangements,
the state of the gear,
whether you have self-steering,
the navigation and communications kit,
how she behaves in a head sea,
and whether she can be sailed short-handed if someone is out of action.

cards.q: How do you plan a watch system for a short-handed crew on a night passage?
cards.a:
Keep watches short enough to stay alert — typically 2 to 3 hours at night — with a clear handover briefing covering position,
course,
traffic,
weather and any changes. Make sure everyone gets sleep before as well as during, and that the skipper is not the only person who can navigate.

cards.q: What should you brief the crew on before a passage?
cards.a:
The plan and the ETA;
the weather;
who does what and the watch system;
lifejackets, harnesses and clipping points;
MOB drill;
how to send a distress call and where the position is displayed;
seacocks, bilge pumps, gas, heads and galley;
fire extinguishers and the liferaft;
and the rule that anyone can raise a concern at any time.

cards.q: What is victualling, and what does a Day Skipper need to think about?
cards.a:
Provisioning for the passage: enough food and, above all, water for the planned trip plus a margin for delay;
food that can be prepared and eaten in a seaway (one-pot meals, sandwiches, soup in a flask made before you leave);
hot drinks;
snacks in the cockpit;
