and allowance for seasickness reducing appetite while dehydration rises.

cards.q: Why make food and hot drinks before you leave harbour?
cards.a: Because cooking in a lumpy sea is difficult, dangerous and the fastest route to seasickness. A flask of soup or stew prepared alongside keeps a cold night watch functioning.

cards.q: What documents should be aboard for a cross-Channel passage?
cards.a:
Passports for everyone,
the ship's registration and Ship Radio Licence,
evidence of VAT status and insurance,
the skipper's certificate of competence and SRC,
a crew list,
and — for France and some other countries — an ICC or national equivalent. Check the current entry requirements before you go.

cards.q: Arriving in the UK from abroad: when does the Q flag go up, and how do you report?
cards.a: Arriving in the UK from outside the UK — the Channel Islands included — you must fly the plain yellow Q flag as soon as you enter UK waters, the 12-mile limit, and keep it up until reporting is complete; failing to do so is a penalty offence. Report through Border Force's sPCR online service, or the C1331 fallback; outbound voyages are notified 2 to 24 hours before departure. Arrivals into Northern Ireland from an EU state need no Q flag. These rules change — check the current gov.uk guidance for both countries before you sail.

cards.q: How do you decide on the day whether to go?
cards.a:
Compare the actual forecast with the limits of boat, crew and passage;
check the tidal windows still work;
look at wind against tide and at the state of the entrance you are leaving and the one you are arriving at;
and consider what happens if the wind is 10 knots more than forecast. The decision to stay in port is a seamanlike decision, not a failure.

cards.q: What do you write in the deck log, and why does it matter?
cards.a:
Time,
position,
log reading,
course steered,
speed,
wind and weather,
barometer,
and events —
sail changes,
engine hours,
fixes,
incidents. It is the raw material for a dead reckoning if the electronics die, and it is the record if anything goes wrong.

cards.q: Preparing for a night passage: what do you do about the navigation lights, your night vision, and the watch?
cards.a:
Do the pilotage plan and all the chartwork in daylight. Check every navigation light and carry spare bulbs; check torches, headtorches and batteries. Set instrument lights to red and keep white deck lights off to protect night vision — 20 minutes to recover it, seconds to lose it. Everyone in lifejackets,
clipped on before leaving the cockpit,
and nobody on deck alone. Hot food and a flask made before dark,
the watch system briefed,
and the log kept every hour so a DR can be started at any moment.

cards.q: How do you register your passage details with the Coastguard?
cards.a: You do not — the old CG66 voluntary safety identification scheme was withdrawn. Instead leave your plan with a responsible person ashore, or use the free RYA SafeTrx app, which records your intended passage and ETA and alerts your emergency contact if you are overdue. Whichever you use, tell them what to do — and what not to do — if you fail to arrive, and always tell them when you get in.

cards.q: How does GNSS work, in one sentence?
cards.a: The receiver measures the time signals from several satellites take to reach it and computes its position from the ranges; four or more satellites give position, altitude and a very accurate time.

cards.q: What are the practical limitations of GNSS?
cards.a:
It can be lost or degraded by antenna failure,
power failure,
jamming or spoofing, and it tells you where you are, not what is around you. Accuracy of a few metres is meaningless if the chart or the datum is less accurate, and the receiver will happily give a position it has interpolated.

cards.q: Why can a GNSS position and a paper chart disagree?
cards.a: Because of the horizontal datum. GNSS works in WGS84; older charts may use a local datum, and the shift can exceed 100 m. Set the receiver to the chart's datum or apply the correction printed on the chart.

cards.q: What is a waypoint, and how should you place them?
cards.a: A position stored in the receiver as a target or a route point. Place them in safe water, not on a buoy or a hazard — never steer straight at a buoy, since everyone else's plotter has it as a waypoint too. Offset them to one side of the mark.

cards.q: What are COG and SOG, and how do they differ from heading and log speed?
cards.a: Course over ground and speed over ground come from the GNSS and include the tide. Heading comes from the compass and log speed from the paddlewheel or ultrasonic log, through the water. Comparing them tells you what the tide is doing.

cards.q: What is 'bearing to waypoint' versus 'course to steer'?
cards.a: The plotter's bearing to waypoint is the direct line from where you are now to the waypoint; it does not allow for tide. A course to steer allows for the tidal stream so you make good the intended track. Steering the bearing to waypoint in a cross-tide sails you round a curve.

cards.q: What does an echo sounder actually measure, and what can fool it?
cards.a:
The time for an ultrasonic pulse to return from the bottom. It can be fooled by a shoal of fish,
a dense layer of weed or plankton,
aeration under the hull from a wave or a turn,
and soft mud giving a reading either above or below the true bottom. It also reads from the transducer, not the keel.

cards.q: What is a lead line, and why would you use one?
cards.a:
A weighted line marked in metres or fathoms, swung ahead and let touch the bottom. It needs no power,
works when the sounder fails,
tells you the nature of the bottom if the lead is armed with tallow,
and is the right tool for sounding out of a dinghy round an unfamiliar anchorage.

cards.q: How does a log measure speed and distance, and what goes wrong?
cards.a: A paddlewheel, impeller or ultrasonic transducer through the hull, calibrated to read speed and to totalise distance. Paddlewheels foul with weed and barnacles and then under-read badly. Check it against GNSS in still water, and know how to clear it — with the bung ready.

cards.q: What can small-craft radar do for you, and what are its limits?
cards.a:
It gives range and bearing of targets and of the coastline in poor visibility, and CPA if it has a plotting function. Limits: a small yacht's scanner is low, so range is short;
sea clutter and rain hide small targets;
targets in a blind sector behind the mast disappear;
and interpreting it takes practice, which is why a radar course is worth doing.

cards.q: What is AIS, and what does it not show you?
cards.a:
Ships broadcast identity,
position,
course,
speed and more over VHF; a receiver shows them with CPA and TCPA. It does not show vessels without AIS — most yachts,
fishing boats,
and anything with it switched off — and it does not show rocks.

cards.q: What is a chart plotter's biggest single danger to a navigator?
cards.a: It shows a small window round the boat symbol, so the wider picture and what lies just off the route disappears. Zoom out regularly, keep a paper chart of the whole passage, and never let the plotter replace thinking about where the dangers are.

cards.q: What is NAVTEX?
cards.a: An automatic text receiver on 518 kHz that prints or displays navigational warnings, weather forecasts and search and rescue information for the area, with no need to be listening at a particular time.

cards.q: Why should you cross-check electronic position with an independent method?
cards.a: Because a single-source position has no error check. Compare the GNSS with a visual fix, a transit, a depth contour or a light bearing. Two independent methods agreeing is a position; one method is an assumption.

cards.q: What is the electrical failure plan on a modern yacht?
cards.a:
Know which instruments are on which circuit and where the breakers and fuses are,
carry spare fuses,
keep the handheld VHF and handheld GNSS charged in the grab bag,
keep a paper chart, almanac, plotting instruments, watch and hand-bearing compass at the chart table,
and log positions regularly so a DR can be started from the last known one.

cards.q: What are the skipper's basic legal responsibilities?
cards.a:
The safety of the vessel and everyone aboard;
compliance with the IRPCS, local byelaws and the law of the country you are in;
keeping the vessel seaworthy and properly equipped;
not going to sea in a manner that endangers others;
and rendering assistance to anyone in distress at sea.

cards.q: What must you do if you receive a distress call?
cards.a: You are obliged to render assistance to persons in distress at sea if you can do so without serious danger to your own vessel or crew. Acknowledge, report to the Coastguard, and proceed if you can help. Do not assume someone else has answered.

cards.q: What may you not discharge overboard?
cards.a: Oil and oily mixtures, and any garbage other than food waste, are prohibited; plastics are banned absolutely. Sewage discharge is regulated and prohibited in many harbours and marinas — use pump-out facilities where they exist. Chemical toilet contents, oil and old antifouling go ashore.

cards.q: What is MARPOL Annex V in practice for a yacht?
cards.a:
Nothing goes over the side except food waste, and only offshore: comminuted food waste, through a 25 mm screen, not less than 3 miles from land; uncomminuted not less than 12 miles, and 12 miles inside a Special Area. Everything else —
plastics,
packaging,
cans,
glass,
oily rags,
filters,
batteries,
flares
— comes back ashore for disposal at the marina's facilities. Boats of 12 m and over must display a placard of the rules.

cards.q: What should you do with out-of-date flares?
cards.a:
Never fire them for fun,
never put them in a bin,
and never leave them at a police or fire station — that is illegal dumping. HM Coastguard no longer accepts flares for disposal. Try the supplier you bought them from,
a liferaft service agent,
your harbour or marina,
a registered disposal point on The Green Blue's environmental facilities map,
a flare amnesty,
or a specialist hazardous-waste contractor for a fee. Disposal is the owner's legal responsibility, so check what is available before you buy new ones.

cards.q: How should you avoid damaging the seabed when anchoring?
cards.a: Avoid anchoring on seagrass beds, maerl and other protected habitats, which chain scours badly; use the designated eco-moorings where they exist; and check the chart and local guidance for protected areas before you drop.

cards.q: What is your responsibility about wash and speed?
cards.a:
Your wash is your responsibility. Slow down past moorings,
dredgers,
works,
small craft,
rowers,
swimmers and anyone working on a boat, and observe harbour speed limits — usually 6 knots or less, and often measured over the ground.

cards.q: How should you behave around marine wildlife?
cards.a:
Do not chase, encircle or separate animals;
keep a steady slow course and let them approach you;
avoid seal haul-outs and nesting seabird colonies, especially in the breeding season;
and give whales and dolphins a wide, predictable berth.

cards.q: What is antifouling and what care does it need?
cards.a: A coating that stops weed and barnacles growing on the hull. It contains biocides, so scrape and sand it only where there is proper containment ashore, wear protection, and never let residues go into the water.

cards.q: What insurance and registration should a cruising yacht have?
cards.a: Third-party liability insurance at the minimum, and usually full cover; many marinas and foreign authorities require proof. Registration (Part 1 or the Small Ships Register) is needed to prove nationality abroad, and a Ship Radio Licence is required for the VHF.

cards.q: What is the ICC and when do you need it?
cards.a: The International Certificate of Competence, issued in the UK by the RYA, is proof of competence recognised by many countries for their inland and coastal waters. It is not needed in UK waters but is often required or requested abroad, and can be obtained on the strength of a Day Skipper practical certificate.

cards.q: What does the RYA Day Skipper practical certificate actually say you can do?
cards.a: That you have been assessed as able to skipper a 30 to 45 ft cruising yacht and its crew safely by day, on day trips, in familiar waters — doing your own pilotage, navigation, boat handling and passage planning. A certificate gained in non-tidal waters is endorsed as such. It is not a licence, and it is not a Yachtmaster.

cards.q: What are the prerequisites for the RYA Day Skipper practical course?
cards.a:
Basic sailing ability plus 5 days at sea, 100 miles logged and 4 night hours aboard a sailing yacht, and navigation and theory to Day Skipper shorebased standard — the shorebased certificate itself is not compulsory. Minimum age 16. The course runs as 5 days,
3 weekends,
or 3 days plus 2.

cards.q: What does the Day Skipper shorebased course cover and how long is it?
cards.a:
About 40 hours plus exam time:
seamanship,
coastal navigation and pilotage,
chartwork,
electronic charts,
position fixing,
plotting a course to steer,
weather and meteorology,
tides,
and the collision regulations. It is assessed by written papers, with chart 5011, an exercise chart and an almanac extract to hand.
